The rows a forecast will need: the next time points of every series

Source: R/ilm_future.R, R/zzz-iml-aliases.R
ilm_future.Rd

Builds a data frame with the next h time points after each series' last observed one, ready to be filled in and forecast. Columns that are constant within each series, such as a site's region, are copied forward. Columns that vary over time are not guessed: they are left missing and named, so that the forecast uses values someone chose, not ones invented here.

Usage

ilm_future(data, time, group = NULL, h = 1L, step = NULL, response = NULL)

Arguments

data

A data frame: the observed history.

time

The name of the time column: numeric, a Date or a date-time.

group

The name of the column identifying each series, or NULL for a single series.

h

How many time points ahead.

step

The step between time points: a number for numeric time or date-times (in seconds), and for dates a number of days or one of "day", "week", "month", "quarter" or "year". By default it is taken from the data.

response

The name of the response column, if data has one. It is left missing without being listed, since it is what the forecast predicts.

Value

A data frame with one row per series and future time point, in the columns of data, plus horizon (1 to h). The names of the columns left missing are in attr(, "unknown"), and the time and series columns in attr(, "time") and attr(, "group"), which ilm_forecast()'s checks read.

Covariates that vary over time

A forecast needs the future values of every covariate the model uses. For some they are known in advance, such as a calendar, a planned dose or a scheduled price. For others they are not, and there are three honest choices:

  • plug in a scenario, and say that is what the forecast assumes;

  • forecast the covariate itself first;

  • supply several plausible paths, so that the forecast's uncertainty includes the covariate's. ilm_covariate_paths() draws them from an illume model of the covariate, and ilm_as_draws() takes them from another tool.

ilm_future() makes none of these choices for you. It leaves those columns missing and names them in a message. A forecast made with realised future values of a covariate is ex-post: in fpp3's terms (section 7.6), made with later information on the predictors, not a genuine forecast. It flatters the model, which is limn's own reading; see ilm_folds().

Time steps

The step between time points is taken from the data unless you give step.

  • For numeric time, it is the one positive difference the series share.

  • For dates, it is a calendar unit when every step is one: a day, a week, a month, a quarter or a year. So monthly dates advance to the same day of the next month, not by a fixed 30 days.

Irregular spacing has no single next time, so then step must be given.

References

Hyndman, R. J. and Athanasopoulos, G. (2021). Forecasting: Principles and Practice, 3rd edition. OTexts. Section 7.6, "Forecasting with regression", ex-ante and ex-post forecasts (online edition, https://otexts.com/fpp3/regression.html#sec-forecasting-regression, read 27 October 2026).

See also

ilm_forecast(), which forecasts the rows; ilm_covariate_paths() and ilm_as_draws() for covariates not known in advance; ilm_folds() for rolling-origin evaluation of forecasts.

Examples

d <- data.frame(site = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 4), month = rep(1:4, 2),
                region = rep(c("north", "south"), each = 4),
                rain = rnorm(8), y = rpois(8, 3))
ilm_future(d, time = "month", group = "site", h = 2, response = "y")
#> These columns vary over time, so their future values are not known: rain. They are left missing: fill them in with the values the forecast should assume.
#>   site month region rain  y horizon
#> 1    a     5  north   NA NA       1
#> 2    a     6  north   NA NA       2
#> 3    b     5  south   NA NA       1
#> 4    b     6  south   NA NA       2
